suffrage

/SUF-rij/ - ends like 'ridge' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Suffrage means the right to vote in political elections.

The museum's centennial exhibit on suffrage displayed the sashes, the petitions, and the first ballot marked by a woman in the county.

Example

For decades the mill town's charter tied suffrage to property, so a foreman who rented rooms above the mill could be taxed for the new bridge but never vote on it; the charter finally fell in 1911.

Suffrage is the right itself — narrower than citizenship, which that foreman held all along, and more concrete than 'political voice.' When histories speak of universal suffrage, they mean one measurable thing: every adult may cast a ballot that counts.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

the franchise: in politics, the legal right to vote — suffrage's nearest twin. Outside politics the word wanders off to business licenses and burger chains; suffrage never wanders — it means the voting right and nothing else.

the vote: the everyday name for the same right — 'women won the vote.' Suffrage is the formal, historical word, the one the movements and the amendments actually used.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disenfranchisement: the stripping away of the right to vote

exclusion: being shut out of political life altogether

Where it sits · how much say citizens hold over how they are governed

petition → suffrage → sovereignty

petition vs. suffrage: Petition is far weaker than suffrage: petitioners may ask and hope while others decide, but suffrage puts the decision itself into the citizen's hands, one ballot at a time.

sovereignty vs. suffrage: Sovereignty goes far beyond suffrage: suffrage gives each citizen a share in choosing who governs, while sovereignty is the supreme authority itself — the final power that answers to no one above it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — suffrage: a vote, the right to vote (Latin suffragium; its deeper roots are debated)

Put it together: Suffrage came into English whole, from Latin suffragium — a ballot, a vote, the right to cast one. Where suffragium itself came from is genuinely uncertain: one ancient guess hears sub- + fragor, 'the crash below' — the roar of shouted approval in a Roman assembly — but the trail is too worn for anyone to be sure. One thing the word never held is suffering: the resemblance is pure accident, and the suffragists chose their banner word because it meant exactly one thing — the vote.

Why there's no relative to spot: Suffragium built almost nothing else in English — suffragist and suffragette are its only working descendants, both coined during the long campaign for the vote, and both still carrying the original meaning on their sleeves.

Strength Check

Word Choice

historical / civic

Suffrage is precise and a little marble-columned: universal suffrage, women's suffrage, the suffrage movement. It names the right, never the act or the paper — you exercise suffrage by casting a ballot, and the ballot is what you drop in the box. And despite the sound, it shares nothing with suffering; a sentence about hardship wants a different word entirely.
